claims.text: Changing the elemental makeup changes the degree of chemical short-range order in nominally single-phase FCC Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-derived alloys.
Differences in chemical short-range order govern the mechanical-property differences among these alloys.
Reducing the constituent count from quinary to quaternary or ternary promotes local chemical ordering.
Enhanced local ordering reduces the effective lattice-distortion barriers that pin dislocations.
The processed equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline is fully single-phase FCC.
The processed equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline is a near-random solid solution with minimal chemical short-range order.
Annealing can be used to enhance chemical short-range order in the investigated alloys.
Chemical short-range order modulates local lattice distortion.
Chemical short-range order modulates dislocation interactions.
A lower constituent count eases chemical differentiation.
Chemically ordered regions exhibit less random lattice distortion.
Chemically ordered regions create a less uniform field of dislocation pinning.
The equiatomic quinary alloy has a more uniform and robust lattice-distortion effect than the lower-constituent alloys.
The quinary alloy's lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and raises yield strength.
Quaternary and ternary alloys will have more chemical short-range order than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Quaternary and ternary alloys with enhanced chemical short-range order will have lower yield strengths than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Enhanced chemical short-range order will modify, and potentially reduce, strain-hardening rates.
Secondary phases or processing-induced defects can dominate the mechanical response outside the proposed scope.
